description: Static daily and stage reference catalog for Baby Log. It supports record review and question preparation only; it does not diagnose, treat, prescribe medication, or decide vaccines.

sources.label: AAP Caring for Your Baby and Young Child, 7th ed.
HealthyChildren: How to Tell if Your Breastfed Baby is Getting Enough Milk
HealthyChildren: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings
HealthyChildren: How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?
HealthyChildren: How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe
HealthyChildren: Back to Sleep, Tummy to Play
HealthyChildren: Safe Sleep Tips for Sleep-Deprived Parents
HealthyChildren: AAP Schedule of Well-Child Care Visits

items.title: 24-hour feeding frequency reference
items.reference_text: Newborns commonly feed frequently. Direct breastfeeding is usually cue-based, often about 8-12 feeds in 24 hours; bottle feeding also commonly needs frequent records.
items.why_it_matters: Feeding frequency helps caregivers and clinicians understand intake rhythm, but it cannot determine adequacy alone; diapers, stools, weight, and alertness matter too.

items.title: No automatic ml estimate for direct breastfeeding
items.reference_text: Direct breastfeeding cannot be measured like a bottle. The app records count, duration, side, and baby state; it does not estimate milk volume from minutes.
items.why_it_matters: Automatic ml estimates create false precision. It is more useful to review feeds, diapers, weight, and clinician assessment together.

items.title: Wet diaper reference for the first 2 days
items.reference_text: In the first 1-2 days, wet diapers and stools may not yet reflect feeding patterns reliably. Record carefully and follow hospital or pediatrician follow-up instructions.
items.why_it_matters: Early intake is small and diaper counts increase gradually; early follow-up helps assess feeding, weight, and jaundice.

items.title: Wet diaper reference for days 3-4
items.reference_text: Around day 3, a common reference is about 4-8 wet diapers in 24 hours.
items.why_it_matters: Wet diapers are one feeding-readiness clue, but should be reviewed with weight, jaundice, alertness, and clinician assessment.

items.title: Stool reference for days 3-4
items.reference_text: For days 3-4, a common reference is about 3-4 loose or seedy stools per day.
items.why_it_matters: Stool color and frequency help observe feeding transition, but should not be used alone to decide abnormality.

items.title: Wet diaper reference after day 5
items.reference_text: After days 5-7, a common reference is 6 or more wet diapers in 24 hours, with urine close to colorless or pale yellow.
items.why_it_matters: Wet diapers are one clue for feeding adequacy. Fewer records do not diagnose a problem, but persistent low counts, dark urine, or caregiver concern should be discussed with a clinician.

items.title: Stool reference after day 5
items.reference_text: After days 5-7, breastfed babies commonly have 3-4 or more yellow, loose or seedy stools per day during the first month.
items.why_it_matters: Stool frequency and texture are feeding-observation clues. Some breastfed babies stool less after 3-6 weeks; review softness, weight, and alertness too.

items.title: Bottle volume reference for the first week
items.reference_text: During the first week, bottle volume per feed is often no more than about 30-60 ml, then gradually increases.
items.why_it_matters: Bottle ml can be counted directly, but actual feeding should follow clinician guidance, hunger cues, and weight changes.

items.title: Bottle volume reference for the first month
items.reference_text: During the first month, bottle amounts gradually increase, commonly reaching about 90-120 ml per feed. Babies vary; follow clinician advice and baby cues.
items.why_it_matters: Bottle volume is countable, but ml alone cannot determine whether feeding is right for the baby.

items.title: Newborn sleep reference
items.reference_text: Newborns commonly sleep about 14-17 hours per day, usually split into many short sessions, with frequent waking to feed.
items.why_it_matters: Sleep records help review rhythm and find forgotten open sessions; they should not pressure a baby into long continuous sleep.

items.title: Safe sleep principles
items.reference_text: Use back sleeping on a firm, flat, separate sleep surface. Avoid soft objects, loose bedding, pillows, bumper pads, and routine bed sharing.
items.why_it_matters: These principles reduce SIDS and suffocation risk. The app only reminds; it does not replace clinician or local safety guidance.

items.title: Awake tummy time reference
items.reference_text: After going home, short supervised tummy-time sessions while awake may start at about 2-3 times per day for 3-5 minutes, then gradually increase toward 15-30 minutes per day by around 7 weeks.
items.why_it_matters: Tummy time supports motor development and helps reduce flat spots. It must be supervised and awake; sleep should still be on the back.

items.title: Temperature red flag under 3 months
items.reference_text: For babies under 3 months, a recorded temperature of 38.0 C or higher should prompt contacting a pediatrician or hospital.
items.why_it_matters: Fever in young infants needs clinician assessment. The app only reminds caregivers to verify the record and contact care; it does not determine the cause.

items.title: First-week well-child follow-up
items.reference_text: AAP well-child schedules include a 3-5 day visit after birth, and many discharge plans call for feeding, weight, and jaundice review within 48-72 hours.
items.why_it_matters: First-week follow-up helps review feeding, weight, jaundice, and screening results. Specific timing should follow the hospital or pediatrician plan.

items.title: Birth-weight return reference
items.reference_text: Early weight loss is common after birth. Clinicians often watch whether weight loss exceeds 10% of birth weight and whether birth weight is regained by around the end of the second week.
items.why_it_matters: Weight change should be reviewed with feeding, diapers, jaundice, and clinician measurements. Family records support questions; they do not replace assessment.

items.title: Development and autism screening reference
items.reference_text: AAP recommends developmental screening during routine care at 9, 18, and 30 months, and autism screening at 18 and 24 months.
items.why_it_matters: This is a visit-preparation reminder. Specific tools and timing should follow the pediatrician.
